stem: The monthly output (in units) of 40 workers in a factory is distributed as follows. Class intervals: 10-20 (frequency 1), 20-30 (frequency 4), 30-40 (frequency 17), 40-50 (frequency 10), 50-60 (frequency 8). Using the assumed-mean method with assumed mean A = 35, compute the coefficient of variation of the output.

per_option_rationale.rationale: Student subtracts instead of adds the correction to the assumed mean: mean = 35 - 10*(20/40) = 35 - 5 = 30. With correct SD=10, CV = (10/30)*100 = 33.33%.
Student omits the correction term -(sum_fd/N)^2 in the variance formula: variance = 10^2*(50/40) = 125 instead of 100. SD = sqrt(125) ~ 11.18. CV = (11.18/40)*100 ~ 27.95%.
Student recovers the coded variance term correctly (var_d = 1.0) but forgets to multiply by h^2=100 when computing actual SD: SD = sqrt(1.0) = 1 (not 10). CV = (1/40)*100 = 2.5%.

explanation_sections.punchline: The assumed-mean method compresses computation, but two traps lurk: the correction term -(sum_fd/N)^2 MUST be subtracted from sum_fd2/N, and SD = h*sqrt(var_d), not just sqrt(var_d).
explanation_sections.approach: Model: grouped data SD via assumed-mean step-deviation shortcut. (1) Compute midpoints and code: d=(m-A)/h. (2) Build fd and fd^2 columns, sum them. (3) Mean = A + h*(sum_fd/N) - ADDITION, not subtraction. (4) Variance = h^2*[sum_fd2/N - (sum_fd/N)^2] - the correction term is the square of the mean coded deviation. (5) CV = (SD/mean)*100. Each step must be executed; skipping the correction term inflates variance by 25%.
explanation_sections.lesson: Variance shortcut: sigma^2 = h^2*[sum(fd^2)/N - (sum(fd)/N)^2]. The term (sum_fd/N)^2 = (correction to mean_d)^2 must NOT be omitted, even when it looks small.
explanation_sections.timing: About 140 seconds. Build the 5-row table first (2 min), then apply formulas. Three traps in order of danger: (a) wrong sign in mean formula gives 33.33%; (b) dropping correction from variance gives 27.95%; (c) forgetting h^2 scaling gives 2.5%.
